newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW -Japan May trade figures.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -Japan May trade figures.

text.p: The following is a selection of economists' and analysts' initial reactions to figures for Japan's May customs-cleared trade surplus, which the government said on Wednesday rose 222.2 percent to 738.27 billion yen:
"The overall surplus was more than the market expected. However, it is likely to keep showing a year-on-year rise in the coming months, but the pace of the increase may slow down.
"The big rise will keep markets worried about renewed trade friction with the United States because Japan's car exports to the U.S. account for a large portion of the overall exports."
"Growth in imports slowed in May due to the April 1 rise in Japan's consumption tax which dampened domestic consumption."
MICHAEL HARTNETT, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH JAPAN:

Commenting on the rise in Japan's surplus with the U.S., he said: "It's the eighth straight month it's up with the U.S. I'm sure the U.S. will bring it up at the G7 meeting but I don't think...they are likely to make anything dramatic out of it. I don't think they will use the yen as a tool with which to beat Japan."
Commenting on the impact of Japan's fiscal tightening on domestic demand, he said: "The U.S. will make damn sure that (Japanese interest) rates don't follow taxes in going up."
"The new story is the dramatic drop we're seeing in rate expectations in Japan...I think the G7 will be quite peaceful and the yen will be sold after the meeting."
KENICHI FUTAKAMI, DAIWA BANK RESEARCH INSTITUTE:

"Japan's surplus is unlikely to keep rising at the rapid pace seen in May partly because companies are cautious about increasing production due to uncertainties about the Japanese economy and Japanese car producers like Toyota and Nissan may try to restrain exports in a bid to avoid trade friction.
"The surplus may end up rising by about 40 percent in 1997/98. The recent rise of the yen may also help curb exports."
